```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6)
```

plateReadeR reads output files from plate readers into a tidy table and offers a few basic quality control (QC) steps. This vignette walks through the whole workflow on a LogPhase600 plate: read, flag, blank-correct, smooth and plot. Joining the data to sample metadata is left to you.

```{r setup}
library(plateReadeR)
```

## Read

Each reader returns one row per well per time point. Time is made relative to the first read and snapped to a regular grid with `snap_hours()`, so that plates from different runs line up exactly.

| Function | Instrument | Format |
|---|---|---|
| `read_logphase_txt()` | LogPhase600 | text, one file per plate |
| `read_logphase_xlsx()` | LogPhase600 | Excel, `Raw Data` sheets, one per plate |
| `read_bioscreen()` | Bioscreen C | UTF-16 text, one or two 100-well plates |

```{r read}
f <- system.file("extdata", "logphase600_plate1.txt", package = "plateReadeR")
d <- read_logphase_txt(f)
d
```

A well is identified by `plate_id` and `well`, in all three readers. `plate_id` is only unique within a run, so add your own run identifier before combining runs, for example with `rbind()`.

## Flag saturated and negative OD

`flag_od_range()` adds well-level flags, so every row of a flagged well carries the flag. There is no default saturation threshold because it depends on your instrument and plate; the value below is only an example.

```{r flag-range}
d <- flag_od_range(d, saturation = 2)
table(unique(d[c("well", "flag_saturated", "flag_negative")])[-1])
```

## Blank-correct

`blank_correct()` subtracts a blank and clips the result at zero. With no `blank` supplied, each well is corrected by the mean of its own first 5 reads.

```{r blank}
d <- blank_correct(d)
d[d$well == "A09", c("hours", "od", "blank_od", "od_corrected")][1:5, ]
```

Alternatively, name blank wells. They are matched by time point within the same plate, and several blank wells on a plate are averaged. (Not run here, because which wells are blanks depends on your plate layout.)

```{r blank-wells, eval = FALSE}
blanks <- data.frame(plate_id = "Plate 1", well = c("A01", "B01"))
blank_correct(d, blank = blanks)
```

## Flag wells that never rise

`flag_no_growth()` flags wells whose corrected OD never climbs more than `min_rise` above its starting level. The default of 0.05 is a starting point: check it against wells you know do and do not grow.

```{r no-growth}
d <- flag_no_growth(d, min_rise = 0.05)
table(unique(d[c("well", "flag_no_growth")])$flag_no_growth)
```

## Smooth

Smoothing is off by default. `smooth_od()` applies a 5-point centered rolling mean to each well. It adds `od_corrected_rollmean`, leaving the raw and corrected columns unchanged. (`blank_correct(smooth = TRUE)` does the same in one step.)

```{r smooth}
d <- smooth_od(d)
names(d)
```

## Plot

`plot_plate()` draws one panel per well for one plate, coloured by QC status. A well with no flags is `"ok"`, and a well with several flags shows them joined with `+`. With `smooth = TRUE` the smoothed curve is overlaid on the raw one.

```{r plot, fig.height = 7}
plot_plate(d, plate = "Plate 1", smooth = TRUE)
```

Because the QC columns are ordinary columns, you can use them to drop wells before further analysis.

```{r filter}
keep <- d[!d$flag_no_growth & !d$flag_saturated & !d$flag_negative, ]
length(unique(keep$well))
```

## A Bioscreen run

`read_bioscreen()` handles the Bioscreen C text export, which is UTF-16 with comma decimals; both are detected and converted for you. A run holds one or two 100-well plates, with wells 1 to 100 on plate 1 and 101 to 200 on plate 2. Wells are named by a zero-padded `well` within each `plate_id` (`"001"` to `"100"`), so the key is the same `plate_id` and `well` pair as for the LogPhase600. The position in the run (1 to 200) is kept as `well_index`. The `Blank` column the instrument writes, which is always zero, is dropped by default.

The file below is a complete two-plate run, 567 reads at about 5-minute intervals over 47 hours, stored xz-compressed (readers can read compressed files directly).

```{r bioscreen-read}
bf <- system.file("extdata", "bioscreen_full.txt.xz", package = "plateReadeR")
b <- read_bioscreen(bf)
b
```

The same QC steps apply. Here the smoothed curve is added during blank correction with `smooth = TRUE`.

```{r bioscreen-qc}
b <- b |>
  flag_od_range(saturation = 2) |>
  blank_correct(smooth = TRUE) |>
  flag_no_growth()

unique(b[c("plate_id", "well", "flag_saturated", "flag_negative", "flag_no_growth")]) |>
  subset(select = -well) |>
  aggregate(cbind(flag_saturated, flag_negative, flag_no_growth) ~ plate_id, data = _, FUN = sum)
```

Wells on a Bioscreen plate are laid out as a square grid of numbers rather than lettered rows, so `plot_plate()` draws them as a 10 by 10 grid.

```{r bioscreen-plot, fig.height = 7}
plot_plate(b, plate = "Plate 2", smooth = TRUE)
```
